A clock is essentially a device that measures time. If you remove the hands from a clock, does it stop being a clock in the sense that it no longer fulfills its purpose? What if you remove the numbers, does the same thing apply? Or what if you remove the clock mechanism that allows the hands to correspond to the correct time (so they just remain static)?

What's the difference between a broken clock and 'not-a-clock' at that point? Is it that a broken clock could be a clock but is missing the correct working components, whereas a 'not-a-clock' was never supposed to be a clock in the first place?

If we were to move beyond clocks I guess the same question still applies – at what point is an object (or person?) no longer itself?
When is a clock still a clock?

Interesting question. Reminds me of a similar conundrum: I own an axe. But the axe head gets damaged so I replace the head. Is it the "same" axe just with a new axe-head? We would probably agree that it is. Then later the handle breaks so I replace the handle. Is it still the same axe, now I have replaced both the head and the handle?

My understanding of these issues is that there is no objective connection between the object and the name, or with concepts like "sameness". The clock is still a clock, even without hands or numerals, if a person names it as such. It is the act of naming an object which creates the connection between the object and the name. Of course, we can debate whether the name is appropriate, but those are arguments about cognitive preferences, not objective reality.

It is the act of naming an object which creates the connection between the object and the name. Of course, we can debate whether the name is appropriate, but those are arguments about cognitive preferences, not objective reality.

The name of the object isn't the same thing as the concept of that object, but the name is what allows us to map that concept to the real-world object. Although the name/symbol, might be arbitrary, I don't think the concept it's mapping to is necessarily arbitrary. There might be no objective connection between the object and the name, but I think there's an objective connection between the object and the concept, a connection that can be subjectively communicated with symbols.
Ok, makes sense, and I disagree that the concept exists objectively, independent of the observer. So in my view, "clock-ness" is an attribute of the observer's cognition, not the physical object.

It's correct every so often, since it could be measuring the time elsewhere on this planet. It's a clock only for that instance of time.

What's the difference between a broken clock and 'not-a-clock' at that point? Is it that a broken clock could be a clock but is missing the correct working components, whereas a 'not-a-clock' was never supposed to be a clock in the first place?

not a Clock -> never be correct in any instance of time.
broken block -> possibly correct in some instance of time.

When they no longer retain the full set of qualities that make them a unique item in intended state.

To me, the real question is "does time exist". Do the hands on a clock or whatever time piece, measure time or is it just a regulated mechanism ticking off (moving) in relationship to something else.
